title: Diwali Lights
strapline: Rows of little lamps glowing in the dark, rangoli patterns bright on the floor — the festival of light comes to the setting.
intent: Diwali, the Hindu, Sikh and Jain festival of lights, celebrates light overcoming darkness and good over difficult times — a warm, joyful theme young children feel long before they can explain it.
Meeting a real celebration from families in the community helps every child see that different homes celebrate in different, wonderful ways, and feel proud when their own festival is honoured.
Making diva lamps, laying rangoli patterns and hanging lights invites rich creative and fine-motor work — moulding, threading, placing, arranging.
Rangoli's repeating shapes and symmetrical patterns are beautiful, hands-on mathematics — pattern, symmetry, and careful arrangement.
The festival grows knowledge of the wider world and the language to talk about it — light, lamp, celebrate, pattern, festival, share.
Sharing sweets, giving cards and lighting the setting together builds belonging, generosity and joyful community.
implementation: Learn about Diwali with the families who celebrate it — invite them to share what they do at home, and follow their lead to keep it accurate and respectful.
Offer clay or dough for making diva lamps (with battery tealights, never real flames), and rangoli-making with coloured rice, petals, chalk or loose parts.
Model the pattern talk: 'Look — you've made red, yellow, red, yellow. What comes next to keep your pattern going?'
Bring in the story of light gently — lamps lighting the way home, the setting glowing warm in the winter dark — and let children fill the room with light.
Weave in maths through the rangoli — symmetry, repeating patterns, counting the lamps, matching the two halves.
Share the joy of the festival together — special sweets or foods (checking allergies and with families), cards to make and give, and music to move to.
key_questions: You've made red, yellow, red, yellow — what comes next to keep your pattern going?
How many diva lamps have we lit in our row?
Can you make both halves of your rangoli match?
What does the light do to the room when it's dark outside?
How does your family celebrate Diwali at home?

impact.text: Children learn about a real festival of light and value that different homes celebrate in different, wonderful ways.
Children make diva lamps and lay rangoli — moulding, threading, placing and arranging.
Children explore symmetry and repeating patterns in the rangoli, and count the lamps.
Children grow words for the festival — light, lamp, celebrate, pattern, festival, share.
Children share sweets, give cards and light the room together, building belonging and generosity.

enhancements: Clay or dough for diva lamps lit with battery tealights, never real flames.
Rangoli-making with coloured rice, petals, chalk or loose parts.
A symmetry challenge — matching the two halves of a rangoli pattern.
Families invited to share what they do at home to keep it accurate and respectful.
Music to move to and special foods to share, checking allergies with families.

playing_exploring: Children explore light, colour and pattern through a real, joyful festival, bringing their own family experiences into the play.
They mould, arrange and create with clay, petals, rice and loose parts.
active_learning: Children take care and pride over their diva lamps and rangoli, working to get the pattern just right.
creating_thinking: Children invent and continue their own patterns and designs, and make sense of a celebration different from or the same as their own.
